Try
TRY
v.t.
From Old French trier, to pick out, to sift. Webster 1828: to examine; to prove by a test; to purify by fire, as metals. In Scripture the word is metallurgical before it is moral: God tries the heart as a refiner tries silver.

Biblical Definition

The Old Testament’s word for trying is a refiner’s word, and God is its subject. Jeremiah states it as a divine prerogative and an inescapable one: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings (Jeremiah 17:10) — and the verse before it is the one that says the heart is deceitful above all things. David invites the same examination on himself: Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart (Psalm 26:2). Peter applies the metaphor to persecution and forbids surprise: think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you (1 Peter 4:12). And John gives the church a duty of trying, with an objective standard: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world (1 John 4:1). The command is addressed to ordinary believers, not to specialists.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TRY as to examine; to prove by a test or experiment; to purify or refine, as metals by fire; to examine judicially; to attempt or endeavor.

TRY, v.t. — To examine; to make experiment on; to prove by a test.

To purify; to refine; as, to try metals by fire.

To examine judicially; to hear and determine a cause.

To attempt; to endeavor; to make an effort.

Old French trier, to pick out or sift — the root of trial and of the winnowing sense in triage.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 17:10 — "I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings."

Psalm 26:2 — "Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart."

1 Peter 4:12 — "Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you:"

1 John 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Modern Corruption

1 John 4:1 commands ordinary Christians to test spiritual claims by doctrine, which is the opposite of the deference that treats a claimed anointing as beyond examination.

expand to see more

Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God. The command is in the plural and addressed to the whole church, the standard given in the next verse is doctrinal (the confession that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh), and the stated reason is that many false prophets have gone out. Nothing in the instruction defers to the claimant’s power, results, sincerity or anointing. This is the standing answer to the culture — found in the New Apostolic Reformation and wherever prophetic office is claimed — in which questioning a leader is treated as touching the LORD’s anointed. The Bereans were called more noble for searching the Scriptures daily to see whether even Paul’s preaching was so (Acts 17:11), and Paul commended them for it.

Jeremiah 17:9-10 must be kept together. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? is immediately answered by I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins. The question is not rhetorical despair; it has an answer, and the answer is God. This is the ground of a properly Reformed self-examination, and it explains why David can pray to be tried rather than dreading it. A man cannot audit his own heart reliably — that is precisely what verse 9 denies — so he submits it to One who can, and asks to be shown. The modern practice of introspection as self-diagnosis attempts what Jeremiah says is impossible; the psalmist’s practice of inviting divine examination attempts what God says He does.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bachan (H974), to examine or prove, as metal; tsaraph (H6884), to refine or smelt; nasah (H5254), to test; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test and approve; peirasmos (G3986), a trial.

expand to see more

Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to try as metal is assayed; I try the reins (Jeremiah 17:10) and try my reins and my heart (Psalm 26:2).

Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to smelt or refine; the refiner’s image behind the whole word-group (Zechariah 13:9).

Hebrew kilyah (H3629) — the reins or kidneys, taken as the seat of the inmost affections.

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test with a view to approval; try the spirits (1 John 4:1).

Greek purosis (G4451) — a burning, a fiery ordeal; the fiery trial which is to try you (1 Peter 4:12).

Usage

"I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins (Jeremiah 17:10) — the answer to the question the verse before it asks."

"Examine me, O LORD, and prove me (Psalm 26:2) — a man submitting what he cannot audit himself."

"Try the spirits whether they are of God (1 John 4:1) — addressed to ordinary believers, with a doctrinal standard."
